power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: Failure to distinguish "mental health" from "mental illness" disrupts effective policy for population well-being

author.affiliation:
Department of Health Policy and Management
								Columbia University

Department of International Health
								Maastricht University

Department of Experimental and Applied Psychology
								Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam

text.text: The semantics and measurement of "mental health", "well-being", and "mental illness" have long been debated -as has the way clinicians and policymakers are expected to respond to their associated insights 1 .
However, despite existing discussion on distinctions between these terms, there is an urgent need to more forcefully articulate how key terminology in mental health should be used.

Failures to do so have been problematic and directly impacted how mental health is understood, which has subsequently impacted efforts to prevent and treat mental illness as well as protect and promote mental health.
Here we highlight significant concerns about incorrect use of these terms, their implications, and why the field needs to urgently apply more stringency in the literature.

Our aim is not to criticize journals, articles, or authors for such mixing, but rather to provide compelling arguments as to why it is critical to be correct and precise about how these are discussed, measured, and addressed to benefit population wellbeing.
Mental health comprises the overall evaluations of lives, functioning, and self-perception, as well as emotional experiences, including happiness, positive affect, meaning, and engagement.
Particularly high levels of this may be referred to as "flourishing" or "thriving", whereas the absence is deterministically poor mental health.

Mental illness explicitly involves the presence of at least one specific mental disorder as defined by evidence-based criteria (such as outlined in the ICD-11 or the DSM 5 TR), which may also extend to extremes (based on number of disorders, type, and/or severity) or, according to some, include personality, addiction, or behavior-based disorders.
Yet, the absence of illness criteria is fundamentally not the equivalent of positive health.
Consider an analogy: not having debts does not make someone financially wealthy, but not having money does make them poor.

The terms "mental health" and "well-being" are often used interchangeably 1 , which is understandable given their measurement, covariates, and associated interventions tend to overlap to the point of indistinction.
However, problematically, "mental health" is also regularly used when the entire focus, including measurements, responses, and implications, are mental illness.
For example, it is not uncommon to see an initiative described as "promoting mental health" when in fact, it is merely focused on recognizing symptoms of depression.

Yet the basic psychological dimensions that make up mental health tend to involve social, functional, and professional assessments 2 , such that improvements involve developing positive relationships, staying connected in public life, or finding meaningful pursuits 3 .
text.formatted: Yet the basic psychological dimensions that make up mental health tend to involve social, functional, and professional assessments <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2</ref> , such that improvements involve developing positive relationships, staying connected in public life, or finding meaningful pursuits <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3</ref> .

text.text: Identifying signs of depression are ultimately for the purpose of intervening therapeutically or clinically.

Independent of the exact lines that distinguish each concept, this misattribution hampers goal-oriented policy debates and targeted research that can inform them by failing to delineate impacts and their driving causes -which can obscure policy solutions.

Additionally, though recent global improvements in recognizing the importance of good mental health and addressing mental illness are remarkable, there are indications that excessive discourse amplifying illness in the context of health may have also created harms 4.
text.formatted: Additionally, though recent global improvements in recognizing the importance of good mental health and addressing mental illness are remarkable, there are indications that excessive discourse amplifying illness in the context of health may have also created harms <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4</ref>.

text.text: The WHO itself regularly uses "mental health" in place of mental illness.
For example, the Mental Health Atlas, and its accompanying World Mental Health Today, focus almost exclusively on prevalence of mental disorders and access to treatment 5, 6 .
text.formatted: For example, the Mental Health Atlas, and its accompanying World Mental Health Today, focus almost exclusively on prevalence of mental disorders and access to treatment <ref type="bibr">5,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">6</ref> .

text.text: A closer look at the language used in WHO documents over time further suggests that, rather than differentiating the two concepts and addressing them as such, there has simply been a shift from using the term mental illness to terming it mental health.

In one instance, WHO itself states that it has long been a supporter of integrating mental health care into primary care -while referring to their own 1995 report on Mental illness in general health care as a key publication in these developments 7 .
text.formatted: In one instance, WHO itself states that it has long been a supporter of integrating mental health care into primary care -while referring to their own 1995 report on Mental illness in general health care as a key publication in these developments <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">7</ref> .

text.text: These patterns are particularly surprising, as their own charter defines mental health as "a state of well-being in which an individual realizes his or her own abilities, can cope with the normal stresses of life, can work productively and is able to make a contribution to his or her community".

In a similar vein, consider that the New England Journal of Medicine (NEJM), arguably the most influential medical publication, has published at least 16 articles with the term "mental health" in the title between 2013 and 2025 (see Supplement Table S1).
text.formatted: In a similar vein, consider that the New England Journal of Medicine (NEJM), arguably the most influential medical publication, has published at least 16 articles with the term "mental health" in the title between 2013 and 2025 (see Supplement Table <ref type="table">S1</ref>).

text.text: Of those, none focused on positive health but instead reported only on illness and treatments.

Likewise, two journals from the Nature publishing group -Nature Health and Nature Mental Health -offered (as of late 2026) 11 categories of article types, of which all are either illness, profession, addiction, or treatment-focused.
In fact, "mental health" was not an option for either journal.
The common debate around "mental health" and "mental illness" generally centers on whether they exist on a single bipolar plane or dual continua (Figure 1a-b) 1, 8 .
text.formatted: The common debate around "mental health" and "mental illness" generally centers on whether they exist on a single bipolar plane or dual continua (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1a-b</ref>) <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">8</ref> .

text.text: We argue that neither depiction is helpful as measurements and remedies for unwanted outcomes are largely distinct.

In other words, lowering rates of mental illness (clinical treatment, active prevention) likely requires a different intervention than improving quality relationships, finding meaningful work, and feeling engaged in daily activities.

The former is more likely to require clinical care while the latter fundamentally requires social/environmental change (e.g., policy, family, personal and professional networks), even if one can benefit the other.
Concurrently, as with physical health, simply not having one specific illness (e.g., depression, anxiety) does not ensure all other dimensions of mental health.
Contrary to Figure 1b, measurement cannot offer a "middle" range for illness; it is either present (to some severity) or not.
text.formatted: Contrary to Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1b</ref>, measurement cannot offer a "middle" range for illness; it is either present (to some severity) or not.

text.text: Instruments such as the Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ) 9 contain gradual symptom levels where "normal" is the only non-illness score and there is no further range to measure positive function.
text.formatted: Instruments such as the Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ) <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">9</ref> contain gradual symptom levels where "normal" is the only non-illness score and there is no further range to measure positive function.

text.text: Measures of mental illness thus essentially start at null and increase with severity once illness is present -even the slightest indication results in a score of "mild", overstating prevalence.

Most people in a population will not truly exhibit the illness, producing a measurement ceiling: no upward movement is possible and no "severity" of positive affect is captured (e.g., feeling calm and peaceful as opposed to feeling worried and unable to rest).

However, the absence of symptoms does not automatically equate to the presence of health: an individual may not suffer from burnout, anxiety, or depression, but this does not guarantee positive relationships, high self-esteem, a strong sense of purpose, or a particularly optimistic outlook.
Likewise, dimensions of mental health (treated synonymously with well-being) can exist positively even in the presence of illness.
Measures of health, however, always span the entire distribution -and have a true "middle" value (i.e., neither exceptionally positive nor exceptionally negative).
Improvement means movement to the right; decline means the opposite.
Yet all individuals exist somewhere.

For illness, there is no "opposite" of having an illness aside from absence: looking for but not finding a tumor provides next to no additional information about an individual's general or positive health.
Thus, Figure 1c demonstrates how 1b should more accurately be depicted.
text.formatted: Thus, Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1c</ref> demonstrates how 1b should more accurately be depicted.

text.text: Literature indicates that the strength (or absence) of inverse correlations should ultimately determine if a single, bipolar model (strong) or dual-continua (weak) approach is more accurate 1 .
However, we argue that both have uses while neither can be fully accurate as the two exist on different planes.
In other words, it is less about whether mental health and mental illness exist on a single or two continua, and more that illness measures cannot explain those for health.
Thus, the conceptual models that have persisted are categorically limited.
Rather than continue to rely on theoretical debates and diagrams, we present what we believe are compelling empirical examples.
These should encourage precision around language that results in greater, intentional distinction between mental health and mental illness.

Figure 2a is the most critical: the two distributions represent over 30,000 individuals from 92 countries that completed the 10-item multi-dimensional psychological well-being scale (MPWB; a validated mental health measure) 2 as well as an adapted PHQ-4 (classic brief measure of mental disorder) 9 .
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">2a</ref> is the most critical: the two distributions represent over 30,000 individuals from 92 countries that completed the 10-item multi-dimensional psychological well-being scale (MPWB; a validated mental health measure) 2 as well as an adapted PHQ-4 (classic brief measure of mental disorder) <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">9</ref> .

text.text: While the health measure shows a robust distribution from most positive to most negative, illness can only range from "normal" to "severe".

Thus, all individuals scoring as "normal" are presumed to be uniformly good mental health, despite the health measure unambiguously indicating otherwise: individuals with a PHQ-4 score of zero covered over 80% of the mental health scale, illuminating heterogeneity that measures of illness fail to detect.
Figure 2b shows the distribution of mental health scores at each point of a granularized PHQ-4 scale (which retains the standard properties but allows a 25-point range).
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">2b</ref> shows the distribution of mental health scores at each point of a granularized PHQ-4 scale (which retains the standard properties but allows a 25-point range).

text.text: For individuals without indications of illness, there is still a wide distribution of health scores; while consistently and significantly lower, the same is true for those at all illness severities.

Figure 2c is therefore a more accurate representation of Figure 1b    1c, the true density and spread of results for mental health and mental illness is concentrated to the positive end, with extreme skew for PHQ.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">2c</ref> is therefore a more accurate representation of Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1b</ref>    <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1c</ref>, the true density and spread of results for mental health and mental illness is concentrated to the positive end, with extreme skew for PHQ.

text.text: Note that scales have been aligned for the two scoring systems to simplify plot (pattern is generally same if using raw values).
In systems where "health care" is often a proxy for "treatment for illness", such distinctions and accuracy are nontrivial and not only about semantics.
To commit to reducing or treating a specific disorder requires an accurate understanding of the illness as well as a common agreement about measurement of its symptoms (to assess affect).
Any system that only examines absence of symptoms is bound to overlook groups and indicators of protective factors for positive outcomes.
It will also miss groups with lower well-being that do not meet the illness threshold but where intervention -primarily in the form of public policy -could prevent illness and promote mental health.

It is not our aim to criticize any specific journal or individual papers; the work is in no way less important based on our arguments nor is it necessary to have consensus agreement on whether the single, bipolar model is more appropriate than the dualcontinua one.

Our goal and recommendation are for institutions, journals, and authors to be much more intentional and rigid on the use terms -if an article includes only measures of mental illness, do not refer to "mental health", or use problematic terms such as "mental health prevention" or "mental health stigma".
Use precise, accurate terms to ensure appropriate insights are gleaned and remedies considered, or demand inclusion of measures that would make those terms appropriate.

A clear distinction provides clarity not only to researchers across fields, but more ably supports policy and decision-makers to identify whether certain findings fall within their remits of introducing change.

Most notably, while an official in the health ministry or a hospital may act on findings in mental illness, professionals in economic and social policy may have opportunities to act on evidence related to promoting mental health and well-being.
That approach and linguistic accuracy has direct benefits toward the public.

Always associating "mental health" with depression or other disorder discourages those working outside healthcare professions to recognize the substantial role they could play toward improving public mental health.
In sum, we argue that to provide both critical aspects, it is the right time to push for semantic and metric precision for the well-being of entire populations.
All members of the Global Mental Wealth 2025 team 2 deserve recognition in contributing to the work that made the empirical examples in this paper possible.
